                 1                                  NOTICE OF MOTION AND MOTION

                 2   TO THE COURT AND ALL PARTIES AND COUNSEL OF RECORD:

                 3          PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that on August 7, 2025, at 2:00 p.m., or as soon thereafter as it may

                 4   be heard, in Courtroom 10 of this Court, located at 450 Golden Gate Avenue, San Francisco, California,

                 5   Defendants Automattic Inc. and Matthew Charles Mullenweg will and do move this Court for an order

                 6   under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) dismissing all claims in Plaintiffs’ First Amended Class

                 7   Action Complaint. Defendants base this Motion on the following grounds:

                 8          Plaintiffs’ claims for intentional interference with contractual relations (Claim 1) and

                 9   intentional interference with prospective economic relations (Claim 2) fail because they do not allege
            10       facts showing that Defendants knew about any of the agreements or prospective economic relationships

            11       at issue, or that Defendants acted with intent to interfere with either.

            12              Second, Plaintiffs’ claim for intentional interference with contractual relations fails for the

            13       additional reason that Plaintiffs fail to adequately allege the contract at issue or how it was disrupted.

            14              Third, Plaintiffs’ claim for intentional interference with prospective economic relations (Claim

            15       2) also fails because the only alleged relationship in the First Amended Complaint is Plaintiffs’ existing

            16       contractual relationship with WPE, which cannot support a separate prospective-interference claim.

            17       Plaintiffs do not identify any other specific third-party relationships from which they derived economic

            18       benefit, nor do they allege facts showing that Defendants intended to disrupt such relationship.

            19              Finally, Plaintiffs’ claim for violation of California’s Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”) (Claim
            20       3) fails for several independent reasons. Plaintiffs lack standing under the UCL because they do not

            21       allege that they “lost money or property as a result of” Defendants’ alleged conduct. Their references

            22       to services disruptions, time spent on mitigation, and speculative expenses do not qualify as economic

            23       injury under the UCL. Plaintiffs are also not entitled to restitution under the UCL because they do not

            24       allege that Defendants obtained any money or property from them. Moreover, Plaintiffs’ UCL claim is

            25       barred because they have not alleged the unavailability of an adequate legal remedy.

            26              This Motion is based on this Notice of Motion and Motion; the following Memorandum of

            27       Points and Authorities in support; the record in this Action; and any other documentary and oral

            28       evidence and argument that may be presented to the Court on this Motion.

                 1                          MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

                 2                                         I.       INTRODUCTION

                 3           Plaintiffs Ryan Keller and Sharon Schanzer allege they are customers of non-party WPEngine,

                 4   Inc. (“WPE”), a company that hosts WordPress websites. They claim Defendants took certain actions

                 5   against WPE that affected WPE’s customers, including them. But Plaintiffs continue to maintain the

                 6   same contractual relationship with WPE that existed before Defendants’ purported actions; their

                 7   businesses remain operational; their websites continue to function; and they retain access to WPE’s

                 8   services. At most, Plaintiffs claim they were inconvenienced because they were worried about how

                 9   their websites and their business could be impacted by what occurred between Defendants and WPE,
            10       and they claim to have taken steps to alleviate those concerns. But even if all of that were true, it doesn’t

            11       mean Plaintiffs have legally cognizable claims against Defendants.

            12               First, Plaintiffs’ claims for intentional interference with their WPE contracts and their

            13       prospective economic relationships with WPE (Count One and Count Two) both fail because Plaintiffs

            14       do not identify whether or how Defendants knew about their WPE contracts or the specific terms at

            15       issue, let alone that Defendants had the requisite intent to interfere with those contracts or relationships.

            16               Second, Plaintiffs’ contractual-interference claim also fails because they do not adequately

            17       allege the terms of their WPE contracts or how, specifically, WPE’s performance of those terms was

            18       hindered or rendered impossible. Defendants identified this fatal flaw in their prior motion to dismiss

            19       Plaintiffs’ original complaint (Dkt. 20), and the First Amended Complaint does little more than add
            20       some technical jargon about service plans that are not clearly tethered to Plaintiffs’ WPE contracts or

            21       any cognizable harm. Plaintiffs also do not identify what, specifically, that jargon means or how

            22       Defendants’ alleged conduct impacted the performance of the terms at issue. To the contrary, Plaintiffs

            23       confirm that WPE found workarounds that allowed Plaintiffs to continue to do business with WPE.

            24               Third, Plaintiffs’ claim for intentional interference with a prospective economic relationship

            25       also fails because the only economic relationship asserted in the First Amended Complaint—the one

            26       between Plaintiffs and WPE—already exists in the form of a contract. Plaintiffs cannot assert a separate

            27       claim on behalf of other potential customers who might have wanted to do business with WPE.

            28               Finally, Plaintiffs’ claim under California’s Unfair Competition Law (Count Three) fails for

                 2   plausible inference that they “lost money or property as a result of” Defendants’ purported actions

                 3   toward WPE. Plaintiffs refer to unspecified “service disruptions” and says they needed to spend time

                 4   addressing them, but none of that amounts to an economic injury sufficient to support standing under

                 5   the UCL. Likewise, Plaintiffs are not eligible for restitution under the UCL because they do not allege

                 6   that Defendants took any money or property from them; there is nothing for Defendants to return in the

                 7   form of restitution. Moreover, Plaintiffs seek equitable remedies but do not allege that their legal

                 8   remedies—namely, money damages—would be inadequate to address any alleged harm here.

                 9            In sum, the First Amended Complaint does not allege any cognizable claim against Defendants
            10       and should be dismissed in its entirety.

            11                               II.      STATEMENT OF ISSUES TO BE DECIDED

            12             1. Whether Plaintiffs sufficiently pleaded their claims for intentional interference with contractual

            13                relations (Count 1) or intentional interference with prospective economic relations (Count 2).

            14             2. Whether Plaintiffs have statutory standing to pursue their UCL claim.

            15             3. Whether Plaintiffs may obtain restitution.

            16             4. Whether Plaintiffs sufficiently pleaded that they do not have adequate remedies at law.

            17                                              III.      BACKGROUND

            18       A.       Factual Background

            19                The following facts, drawn from the First Amended Complaint, are taken as true for purposes

            20       of this motion only. Defendant Automattic Inc. and its CEO, Defendant Matthew Mullenweg, are key

            21       contributors to and stewards of the WordPress ecosystem, an open-source content management system

            22       on which millions of websites globally rely. First Amended Complaint (FAC) ¶¶ 2, 22, 24. Automattic

            23       operates services including WordPress.com, WordPress VIP, and Pressable, while also contributing to

            24       the open-source infrastructure maintained via WordPress.org. Id. ¶¶ 15, 23, 25, 29-30. The WordPress

            25       software is free and open-source, and no users—including Plaintiffs and WPE—have paid Defendants

            26       for use of the software distributed via WordPress.org. Id. ¶¶ 2, 44.

            27                WPE is a “managed website hosting” company that sells its hosting platform, plugins, themes,

            28       support, and other tools to customers like Plaintiffs to handle the technical aspects of running a

                 6                                       IV.        LEGAL STANDARD

                 7           A motion to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) “tests the legal sufficiency

                 8   of a claim.” Navarro v. Block, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001). Dismissal is warranted when a

                 9   plaintiff fails to provide “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.” Bell Atl.
            10       Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007); see Ixchel Pharma, LLC v. Biogen, Inc., 821 F. App’x

            11       897, 898 (9th Cir. 2020) (mem.) (affirming dismissal of intentional-interference claims). “Dismissal

            12       under Rule 12(b)(6) is proper when the complaint either (1) lacks a cognizable legal theory or (2) fails

            13       to allege sufficient facts to support a cognizable legal theory.” Somers v. Apple, Inc., 729 F.3d 953,

            14       959 (9th Cir. 2013). While allegations of material fact are assumed to be true and viewed in the light

            15       most favorable to the plaintiff, mere “conclusory allegations of law and unwarranted inferences are

            16       insufficient to defeat a motion to dismiss.” Adams v. Johnson, 355 F.3d 1179, 1183 (9th Cir. 2004);

            17       accord Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009).

            18                                                 V.      ARGUMENT

            19               The fundamental defect here is Plaintiffs’ failure to connect any actionable disruption of their
            20       WPE contracts with anything Defendants knew about or intended to do. Plaintiffs don’t allege that

            21       Defendants were aware of any of the specific terms of their WPE contracts; they don’t allege how

            22       Defendants’ alleged conduct toward WPE impacted the performance of those terms; they don’t allege

            23       that Defendants knew about or intended to bring any of that disruption about; and they don’t allege

            24       what money or property they supposedly lost as a result. At best, Plaintiffs point to business decisions

            25       they voluntarily made due to concerns about WPE’s reliability, but that alone cannot support any of

            26       the claims asserted in the First Amended Complaint.

            27               A. Plaintiffs fail to plausibly allege either of their intentional-interference claims

            28               Both of Plaintiffs’ intentional-interference claims (Counts One and Two) fail as a matter of law

                 1   because: (1) they do not adequately plead Defendants’ knowledge of their contracts and the specific

                 2   terms at issue, let alone intent to interfere and actual resulting disruption; and (2) they fail to identify

                 3   any prospective economic relationship that they would have benefitted from.

                 4                  1. The elements of Plaintiffs’ intentional-interference claims

                 5          In California, a claim for intentional interference with contract requires a plaintiff to allege:

                 6   “(1) a valid contract between plaintiff and a third party; (2) defendant’s knowledge of this contract; (3)

                 7   defendant’s intentional acts designed to induce a breach or disruption of the contractual relationship;

                 8   (4) actual breach or disruption of the contractual relationship; and (5) resulting damage.” CRST Van

                 9   Expedited, Inc. v. Werner Enters., Inc., 479 F.3d 1099, 1105 (9th Cir. 2007).

            10              A claim for intentional interference with prospective economic relations has similar elements;

            11       a plaintiff must allege “(1) an economic relationship between the plaintiff and some third party, with

            12       the probability of future economic benefit to the plaintiff; (2) the defendant’s knowledge of the

            13       relationship; (3) intentional acts on the part of the defendant designed to disrupt the relationship;

            14       (4) actual disruption of the relationship; and (5) economic harm to the plaintiff proximately caused by

            15       the acts of the defendant.” Id. at 1108. And with a prospective-economic-relations claim, the plaintiff

            16       must also allege that the defendant’s conduct was independently wrongful—i.e., that it is “wrongful by

            17       some [legal] measure beyond the fact of the interference itself.” Id. (cleaned up).

            19                         economic relationships

            20              To allege a cognizable claim for intentional interference with a contract (Count One) or

            21       intentional interference with a prospective economic relationship (Count Two), Plaintiffs must plead

            22       sufficient facts to establish that Defendants were aware of and intended to interfere with those

            23       relationships, and that some actual interference resulted. See Swipe & Bite, Inc. v. Chow, 147 F. Supp.

            24       3d 924, 935 (N.D. Cal. 2015). Here, at most, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants took some actions meant

            25       to affect WPE—but that is a number of significant steps removed from a viable claim that Defendants

            26       knew about, intended to interfere with, and did interfere with Plaintiffs’ specific contracts or their

            27       unidentified prospective economic relationships.
